summary: Defines the MESSAGE method, an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol that lets instant messages be sent between users in near real time. The messages are usually short and used conversationally. It gives SIP a basic way to carry text chat without setting up a session.

eli5.summary: This lets people send quick text notes to each other using the same system that sets up phone calls over the Internet, like sending a text message.

subtitle: A SIP method for sending stand-alone instant messages, like pager messages, through the existing SIP network.

tldr.problem: SIP could set up sessions and handle presence, but had no way to carry an instant message. Existing instant messaging protocols were proprietary, which hampered interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The MESSAGE method carries the message as a MIME body in a SIP request that follows normal SIP routing and security. Each message stands alone and does not create a dialog.
tldr.outcome: SIP gained a pager-style messaging method with size and congestion rules and strong security requirements. It has since been updated by RFC 8591.

today: RFC 3428 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8591. Read the two together for the current rules.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs a MESSAGE Method
sections.content:
Instant messaging (IM) is the exchange of content between participants in near real time. It is usually short text, grouped into brief live conversations of many small messages, which is how it differs from email in common usage.

The RFC notes that the protocols for IM combined with presence and buddy lists were all proprietary, which had seriously hampered interoperability. SIP already helped with presence and session-oriented communication, but not with instant messages. RFC 3428 fills that gap with a new SIP method called MESSAGE, whose request normally carries the message in its body.

Implementations MUST support the instant message requirements of RFC 2779 that fall within the RFC's scope. RFC 2778 and RFC 2779 give the model and requirements for presence and instant messaging.
sections.eli5: Chat programs used to talk only to their own kind. This RFC adds a 'send a note' button to SIP, a language many programs already speak.

sections.title: Scope: The Pager Model
sections.content:
The RFC covers only the pager model, similar to a two-way pager or an SMS handset. There is no explicit association between messages: each IM stands alone, and any sense of a conversation exists only in the client user interface. The contrasting session model has a clear beginning and end, which in SIP would be a media session started with an INVITE and ended with a BYE. The RFC says the SIMPLE work group planned to address IM sessions in a separate document.

The RFC argues against faking a session by opening a dialog and sending MESSAGE requests inside it. Such requests would follow the same network path as other SIP requests even though they carry media, and IM volume is typically high, so there could be congestion problems if a hop forwards a request over UDP. Implementations SHOULD NOT create dialogs for the primary purpose of associating MESSAGE requests with one another.

Sending a MESSAGE inside an existing dialog is still allowed, for example when one participant in a voice session wants to send an IM tied to that session.
sections.eli5: This is for sending single notes, like pager beeps, not for a long phone-style chat with a start and an end.

sections.title: How a MESSAGE Travels
sections.content:
The sender issues a SIP request with the MESSAGE method. The Request-URI is normally the recipient's address of record, but may be a device address if the client knows the recipient's current location. The body can be of any MIME type, including message/cpim, a format expected to be supported by other IM protocols so that endpoints using different protocols can exchange messages without gateways changing the content.

The request may cross a set of SIP proxies and transports. Provisional and final responses return to the sender as for any other request. Normally a 200 OK is generated by the user agent of the final recipient, which means the user agent accepted the message, not that the user has seen it. MESSAGE requests do not establish dialogs.

A proxy routes a MESSAGE by the usual SIP rules and may fork it to several terminals. Even if several deliveries succeed, a forking proxy forwards only one final response upstream, so the sender cannot tell whether a fork happened.
sections.eli5: You hand a note to the post office, it passes through a few sorting stations, and the person's phone says 'got it'. That means it arrived, not that they read it.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Rules
sections.content:
A sender (UAC) that supports MESSAGE MUST be prepared to send a body of type text/plain, and may send message/cpim. A UAC MUST NOT insert a Contact header field into a MESSAGE. It MAY add an Expires header field to limit the validity of the content, and if it adds a non-zero value it SHOULD also add a Date header field.

The receiver (UAS) SHOULD respond with a final response immediately, and is not obliged to display the message. A 2xx response MUST NOT contain a body, and a UAS MUST NOT insert a Contact header field into it. A UAS MUST be prepared to receive and render text/plain bodies, and may support message/cpim.

  • 200 OK: delivered to the final destination, but the user may not have read it.
  • 202 Accepted: handed to a gateway or store-and-forward service, so delivery is not guaranteed. A relay SHOULD return this.
  • 4xx or 5xx: not delivered successfully.
  • 6xx: delivered, but refused.

A message is expired when the time in its Expires header field has passed, counted from the Date header field or from when the UAS received it. What to do with an expired message is left to local policy. If it is displayed, the UAS SHOULD clearly mark it as expired.

Recipients can be named with an Instant Message URI of the form im:user@domain. A UA SHOULD resolve it to a SIP URI before sending, so that proxies unaware of the im: namespace can route normally. Record-Route and Route header fields MUST NOT contain IM URIs.
sections.eli5: The sender must be able to write plain text and must not leave a return address on the note. The receiver answers quickly with a code: 'got it', 'passed it along', 'failed' or 'refused'.

sections.title: Size Limits and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Unlike most SIP requests, MESSAGE requests carry media (the IM itself) rather than signaling about media. If a SIP network is shared between call signaling and IM, heavy IM traffic could interfere with call signaling.

MESSAGE requests SHOULD be sent over transports with end-to-end congestion control, such as TCP or SCTP. Since SIP cannot stop a downstream hop from using UDP, the RFC adds a size cap: a MESSAGE outside a media session MUST NOT exceed 1300 bytes, unless the UAC knows the message will not cross a congestion-unsafe link, or that it is at least 200 bytes smaller than the lowest MTU on the path. Larger payloads may go in a media session or use content indirection.

A UAC MUST NOT start a new out-of-dialog MESSAGE transaction to a URI while a previous one to the same URI is pending. Inside a dialog it SHOULD NOT overlap transactions, and MUST NOT unless every hop of the route set uses a congestion-controlled transport. Because a request and its response must cross the whole path, this slows new messages when the network becomes congested.
sections.eli5: If everyone sends big notes at once, the post office jams. So notes must be small, and you wait for an answer before sending the next one to the same person.

sections.title: Method Definition and Example Flow
sections.content:
The method name MESSAGE is case sensitive. The RFC extends the header field tables of SIP with a MESSAGE column showing which header fields are mandatory, optional or not applicable. Call-ID, CSeq, From, To, Max-Forwards and Via are mandatory in a MESSAGE request.

The worked example sends a request from User 1 to User 2 in the same domain through one proxy. The request has Content-Type: text/plain and the body Watson, come here. The proxy looks up User 2 in its registration database, forwards the request, and passes the 200 OK back along the Via path. Most header fields are reflected in the response.
sections.eli5: The example is one person sending 'Watson, come here' through a middleman to a friend, and the friend's phone saying OK back the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In most SIP requests the real communication happens in a media session. With MESSAGE the payload is the communication, so the need for security is greater. UAs supporting MESSAGE MUST implement end-to-end authentication, body integrity and body confidentiality mechanisms.

  • Outbound authentication: proxy authentication is RECOMMENDED when local proxies carry outbound messages, to verify the originator and limit spoofing and spamming.
  • SIPS URIs: they ask for a secure connection on every hop, but users must trust each proxy, and unencrypted bodies are visible to proxies. A forking proxy can also deliver to endpoints the sender did not intend.
  • End-to-end: bodies MUST be secured with S/MIME. Endpoints MUST support encryption (CMS EnvelopedData) and S/MIME signatures (CMS SignedData).
  • Replay: signed requests and responses MUST contain a Date header field covered by the signature. A message dated several minutes too old or too new SHOULD get a 400 response. This does not work for devices without clocks, and stale dates are normal for store-and-forward delivery.

A signed message/cpim body can protect metadata such as the sender across a gateway to another CPIM-compliant service that does not understand SIP header fields.
sections.eli5: Since the note itself is the message, it needs a sealed, signed envelope that only the right person can open, and a date stamp so nobody can resend an old note.
